A specific texture associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers
I drift off into a world of my own
make sure never to be alone with another person

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
I feel like an object, not like a person
You can never know who will harm you

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Threat: missing/none selected despite multiple current-danger and exposure-related items
issues.explanation: The profile contains several items implying an active sense of present threat or exposure (e.g., 'World is Dangerous', 'Exposed to Others', concealment to avoid being noticed), yet the Threat component is entirely absent. For this trauma type, such items would usually cohere with at least some explicit threat content; the omission makes the cross-node picture clinically uneven.

'World is Dangerous' expresses a broad ongoing threat belief, but the formulation specifies no active links into or out of Threat and no Threat items are endorsed. This makes the appraisal sit awkwardly in the formulation because it functions more like a threat belief than an isolated negative self-appraisal.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
issues.explanation: 'Concealing Clothing ... to avoid being noticed' implies active management of current interpersonal threat/visibility. With Threat completely unrepresented and no Trigger→Threat or Maladaptive Strategies→Threat linkage in the formulation, this strategy lacks a clear matching symptom target in the rest of the profile.

Threat: missing/none selected despite multiple current-danger and exposure-related items

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: The Threat node is not clinically coherent here. 'Flashbacks' and 'Physical Reactivity' are re-experiencing/arousal responses rather than threat appraisals, while the only genuine threat appraisal selected is 'Threat from Strangers.' That mixes different constructs within one node.

vignette: Ethan, a 25-year-old North American man, had experienced severe physical abuse at the hands of his caregiver during childhood. This traumatic event left deep scars that he carried into adulthood and now manifested in various symptoms of PTSD. The nightmarish experience began when Ethan was just a child. His caregiver would often lash out violently without warning, leaving him with bruises and cuts that were too numerous to count. These episodes usually occurred late at night, often when it was dark outside or when Ethan woke up feeling alone in the darkness. One particular tactile trigger, the texture of his caregiver's rough hands gripping his skin, still haunted him deeply. The sounds of children crying would also instantly bring back those painful memories. As an adult, these triggers continued to affect him profoundly. Nighttime and darkness were particularly terrifying for Ethan; he often found himself waking up in a cold sweat, feeling as though the abuse was happening all over again. The memory replayed vividly in his mind, like a film that played endlessly, each frame re-enacting the trauma with full sensory intensity. Ethan's occupation as a housekeeper provided him with little respite from these triggers. He found himself frequently avoiding tasks that required working alone late at night or dealing with clients whose rough hands reminded him of those painful moments. His maladaptive strategies included dropping important responsibilities to avoid potential triggers, which resulted in conflicts with his employers and colleagues. To cope with the overwhelming emotions triggered by memories, Ethan often drifted into a world of his own, escaping through fantasies that provided temporary relief from reality. He never felt safe being alone, constantly ensuring there was someone else around him for company. This need to be "never alone" had strained many personal relationships over time. Ethan's negative appraisals about himself and the world were deeply ingrained. He believed that others could see the abuse in his eyes or through other subtle signs on his body, leaving him feeling exposed and vulnerable. His sense of self was fragmented; he often felt like an object rather than a person with agency and worth. The fear of harm lingered constantly-anyone could be a potential threat. The physical reactivity to triggers was intense. He would break out in cold sweats or experience rapid heartbeats whenever something reminded him of the stressful event. His hypervigilance had made daily life exhausting, as he remained on high alert at all times, always scanning his environment for signs of danger. It wasn't until one particularly overwhelming flashback while working alone late at night that Ethan finally decided to seek help. The memory replayed so vividly that he felt like the abuse was happening again, and he froze in panic. This episode left him feeling completely shattered and helpless. He realized that his maladaptive strategies were no longer sustainable and that his fear of being alone or dealing with triggers had taken over almost every aspect of his life. Ethan hoped to find a way to reclaim control over his emotions and daily functioning. He was most afraid that the trauma would continue to dictate how he lived, but he also held onto hope for a future where he could feel safe, connected, and whole again. Seeking therapy represented a significant step towards addressing these fears and rebuilding a life free from constant reminders of his childhood abuse.
